title: The Power and Limits of Decision Making with Confounded Data: The Case of Pricing
contribution: Shows that the optimal price cannot be identified from confounded observational data, bounds the true-profit ratio of the predictive (plug-in) price under three conditions on pricing data, and builds a bootstrap-calibrated test of whether any data-driven decision is distinguishable from optimal; on auto-loan data the test rejects the predictive rules in 9 and 13 of 16 segments but a propensity-score prescriptive rule in only 2.
problem_entry: {DA AP} Operational data are mostly observational, so historical prices and demand may be confounded and usually lack confounders or an instrument (pp. 1-3); practice optimizes the prediction of demand given price instead of the causal demand curve (pp. 4-5); entry point: only the objective value of the final decision matters, stated as a display line (p. 3).
key_idea: Power side: bound R(z~)/R(z*) for the predictive price using the structure of pricing and of pricing data (Theorems 2-4, pp. 13-15). Limits side: test H0: R(z*) = R(z^) for any data-driven rule where covariates identify the optimum, with a partial-means kernel optimum, a chi-squared null and a bootstrapped scale (pp. 15-27). A parametric prescriptive rule by generalized propensity score is added (pp. 27-28). Change from Besbes-Phillips-Zeevi (2010): causal instead of predictive objective, observational instead of experimental data (pp. 15-16, fn. 3).
assumptions: One price, profit z - c, potential demands, iid (Z, Y^obs) (p. 4). Bounds: linear non-increasing mean demand plus confounding error bounded relative to market size (Thm 2, p. 13), jointly normal with non-positive correlation (Thm 3, p. 14) or non-increasing in price (Thm 4, p. 15). Test: weak ignorability given X (p. 19), kernel and bandwidth conditions called a choice rather than an assumption (pp. 22-23), unique interior optimum and regularity (p. 23), a rule converging slightly faster than the kernel optimum (p. 25). Data: simulated confounded instance (p. 29) and Columbia CPRM auto loans in 16 segments (pp. 17, 31-32); ignorability for six covariates argued, not tested (pp. 32-33).
proof_devices: two-model parable: Alice's and Bob's complete potential-outcome models reproduce the observed price-demand table but give different optimal prices (pp. 8-10)
Theorem 1: non-identifiability of the optimal decision even under the Gauss-Markov assumptions (pp. 10-11)
confounding error E(z) = E[eps | Z = z] as the gap between predictive and causal demand (p. 11)
extreme-maximizer sandwich: worst-case error functions reduced to monotone step functions at +-eta (proof of Theorem 2, pp. 38-40) and to constants under monotone confounding (Theorem 4, p. 41)
each bound checked on a worked curve: 0.71 <= 0.75, 0.94 <= 0.96, 0.79 <= 0.84 (pp. 14-15)
identification by iterated expectations under weak ignorability (eq. 3, Theorem 5, p. 20)
partial-means Nadaraya-Watson estimator with asymptotics via Newey (1994) Theorem 4.1 (Theorem 6, pp. 22-24, 41-43)
three-term decomposition of the test statistic after Besbes et al. (2010) (Theorem 7, pp. 25, 44)
bootstrap of an asymptotically pivotal term for the unknown scale (Theorem 8, pp. 26-27)
conservative p-value by stochastic dominance of a weighted sum of two chi-squared variables (Theorem EC.1, pp. 46-47)
experiments: Simulated example: predictive price 4.330 earns zero true profit against an optimum of 31.25 at 2.5 (p. 30); 256 replicates per sample size, the test reaches its 5% size after a few hundred observations (p. 31); bandwidth constants given without a selection rule (p. 30). Auto loans, 16 segments, n = 690-4,495, B = 100: rejections at p < 0.05 in 9/16 (parametric predictive), 13/16 (non-parametric predictive) and 2/16 (prescriptive parametric) segments (Table 4, p. 32; p. 33); the prescriptive rule recoups 70% and 36% of the predictive rules' lost profit (p. 34). No software or run times reported.
positioning: Extends the objective-optimality test of Besbes, Phillips and Zeevi (2010) from experimental and predictive settings to observational data and causal effects, reusing their auto-loan setting and estimators (pp. 15-17, 31-32); endogeneity work in econometrics frames the problem (p. 3); Hirano-Imbens propensity scores and Newey partial means are the tools (pp. 19, 23, 27); pricing by repeated experimentation (Bertsimas-Perakis 2006, Besbes-Zeevi, Nambiar et al.) is set aside (p. 2). Within the skill: practice side of Tension T3 (no LP, conic or MIO step) and slow-pipeline side of T5 (arXiv 2016 to IJOO 2023, per card S223).
writing: Thesis set off as a display line (p. 3); a running MIT Coop hoodie parable with two consultants (pp. 4-10, 20-21); every bound checked numerically on a worked curve (pp. 14-15); the power/limits frame repeated in title, overview and conclusion (pp. 7, 34); an abstract slip, 'even when data is unconfounded' (p. 1).
limits_future: Bounds only for pricing with linear non-increasing demand (pp. 13-15); confounding size neither known nor estimable (p. 14); the test works only where H0 is identifiable, via ignorability argued but not tested for the loan data (pp. 17, 32-33); the null is not expected to hold exactly and the bar should rise with n (pp. 33-34); no software or run times. Future: structure-based bounds for other observational decision problems (p. 13). The abstract's 'even when data is unconfounded' contradicts its thesis (my reading, p. 1).

method_links.note: Decisions are scored by true profit, not model fit; H0 is stated in terms of the decision's revenue (p. 16). The baselines are the incumbent study's own predictive regressions, data, segments and profit function (Besbes et al. 2010), re-tested under the causal objective.

Optimality-ratio curves in one knob gamma (Figure 2), but gamma measures confounding that no decision-maker sets and that is neither known nor estimable; Theorem 3 swaps it for a ratio that can be estimated. Same reading as card S223.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: H0: R(z*) = R(z^) is tested by the gap between a partial-means kernel optimum and the rule's decision, both scored by the kernel objective, against a chi-squared null with a bootstrapped scale; EC.2 gives a conservative p-value when the rule converges no faster than the kernel optimum. Same device as card S223.
Alice's and Bob's complete demand models both reproduce the observed price-demand table yet recommend $20 and $28; a home-game covariate with ignorability then selects Bob's model.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: assume only what can be estimated, worst-case the rest
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theorem 3 replaces the unknowable confounding size of Theorem 2 by average demand relative to market size, which can be estimated by the sample average of observed demand.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: multiplicity check before reading segment rejections
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Before reading the prescriptive rule's 2 rejections in 16 segments, the authors note that a true null would produce two or more rejections about 19% of the time, and that the null is not expected to hold exactly.

transferable: To show an optimal decision is not identifiable, build two complete potential-outcome models that reproduce the observed joint distribution exactly but imply different optimal decisions; then show which covariate, with ignorability, singles one out (Tables 2-3, pp. 8-10, 20-21).
Bound a plug-in decision's true-objective ratio by computing the extreme maximizers over all admissible model errors, after reducing those errors to step or constant functions at +-eta (pp. 38-41).
When a test statistic's scale is a nuisance, bootstrap an asymptotically pivotal companion quantity instead of estimating densities and second derivatives (Theorem 8, pp. 26-27).
Before reading k rejections across m segments, compute their chance under a global null: with 16 segments at alpha = 0.05, two or more rejections occur about 19% of the time (p. 33).
Re-test an incumbent study inside its own setting (its data, segments, estimators and r(z) = z - 2%) so that a different conclusion cannot be blamed on the setup (pp. 31-32).
coauthors: Nathan Kallus (Cornell Tech and Cornell University) (p. 1)

quotes.text: predictive models may give biased causal estimates but still lead to good decisions.

Note that if the null hypothesis were actually true in all 16 segments (i.e., our prescriptive parametric approach is revenue optimal), we would still reject the null in two or more segments about 19% of the time.

title: Multiperiod and Online Optimization for Fleet Defense: Centralized and Distributed Approaches
contribution: Solves the exact nonlinear mixed-binary fleet-defense (weapon-to-target) model online with closed-form lazy tangent cuts (about 99 times faster to the optimum and about 32 times faster to proof than the binary SOCP), extends it to multiperiod raids with destruction indicators, and designs a three-step robust protocol with optimized messages that secures more ships than no communication, all on synthetic instances.
problem_entry: {IO RO AP; CP for the conic reformulation} Ships must assign hard-kill and soft-kill weapons to threats, maximizing survival and saving weapons (pp. 1-2); the predecessor (Becker et al. 2013) solves the exact binary SOCP offline only, uses a linearized heuristic online, and its distributed protocol broadcasts too much data (p. 3); the convex formulation of Ahuja et al. is described as intractable at 20 weapons x 20 threats (p. 2).
key_idea: LAZY: drop the product constraints and add closed-form tangent hyperplanes as lazy cuts (Algorithm 1, Lemma 1, pp. 9-10); multiperiod model with binary destruction indicators, re-solved after each raid (pp. 10-13); decentralized protocol in three steps: each ship's own MIO chooses which messages to broadcast under a budget, ships broadcast, then each re-solves a robust problem over what it was not told (pp. 13-19).
assumptions: Threat lethality 1; centrally, common knowledge of targeting and accurate efficacies (p. 5); probabilities in [eps, 1 - eps] (p. 7); independent hard-kill weapons and at most one soft-kill weapon per threat (pp. 5, 7); survival thresholds, priorities and a large slack penalty (p. 6). Protocol for one attack and hard-kill weapons only, with global vs private data (p. 14). Data: synthetic scenarios modelled on Becker et al., efficacies uniform on ranges such as [0.5, 1] (pp. 22-28); no fleet data.
proof_devices: nonlinear constraints of the form 1 <= prod u_i, convex and rotated-SOC representable (p. 8)
LAZY outer approximation by lazy constraints with tolerance delta (Algorithm 1, p. 9)

Lemma 1: closed-form tangent separating hyperplane sum x_i/yhat_i = n at the radial or the orthogonal projection (pp. 9-10; proof by tangent plane and by KKT with bisection on one multiplier, pp. 41-42)
big-M links between survival slacks and destruction indicators in the multiperiod model (pp. 11-12)
binary broadcast variables under a message budget that linearize companions' destruction probabilities (pp. 15-16)
box uncertainty whose robust counterpart is the nominal problem at the upper bound Q^ (pp. 17-18)
Proposition 1 by feasibility carry-over from Step 1 to Step 3: z3(s) <= z1(s) (p. 20; pp. 42-43)
parallel race of nine cut variants, stopping at the first proof of optimality (p. 23)
experiments: Julia/JuMP, Gurobi 6.5, 16 GB (p. 22). MIO vs the authors' GREEDY on 1,000 random instances: identical 46%, GREEDY worse 54%, 14.5% more weapons, 3.5% with ships left insecure (p. 22). Parallel lazy cuts vs binary SOCP: optimum found 3.93 s vs 389 s (reported 98.9x), proof 16.91 s vs 545 s (about 32x, my arithmetic); run count not stated (p. 23; Tables 2-3, pp. 35-36). 95% quantiles over 1,000 instances: proof within 30.2 s in one-ship sensitivity cases (Table 4, p. 37), 63 s at 8 ships, 40 hard-kill weapons, 24 threats (Table 5, p. 38). Multiperiod vs myopic: 3.59 vs 3.17 ships, 0.17 vs 0.45 weapons wasted, the multiperiod method seeing future raids' data (Table 6, p. 39; pp. 26-27). Protocol (budget 2) vs none vs centralized: 3.2 / 2.15 / 4.94 ships, 14.96 / 12.6 / 11.58 weapons (Table 7, p. 40; pp. 28-29). Synthetic data only.
positioning: Builds on Manne (1958) and the weapon-target literature (Ahuja et al. 2007; Hosein-Athans 1990; auction, greedy and simulated-annealing heuristics) (pp. 1-3) and directly on Becker et al. (2013), an MIT Lincoln Laboratory working paper co-authored by Bertsimas, which it generalizes and whose protocol it criticizes for message volume (pp. 3-4, 13, 19, 31); multi-agent optimization (Terelius et al. 2011; Lobel et al. 2011) named as a transfer target (p. 4).
writing: Four numbered contributions mapped to sections, with a claim of transfer to other problems (pp. 3-4); a quantile table turned into an operator's stop rule (p. 24); a discussion section restating the contributions (pp. 29-30); slips: 'Sections 2 and 2' (p. 4), mu vs nu for the companion penalty (pp. 15-16, 28), '2.5Hz processor' (p. 22).
limits_future: Centralized model ignores data locality and is slow (p. 29); protocol only for one attack and hard-kill weapons (p. 14); the protocol spends more weapons (pp. 20, 29); synthetic instances only; no convergence or complexity result for LAZY, so the abstract's proof claim rests on Lemma 1 and experiments (my reading, pp. 1, 9, 22-26); the communication budget is not varied (p. 28). Future: the lazy-cut and multiperiod devices for transportation with nonlinear effects and resource allocation, communication variables for multi-agent optimization (p. 4); the conclusion names no open problem (p. 30).

method_links.note: The exact nonlinear mixed-binary model stays in a solver class (convex, rotated-SOC representable, solved by lazy linear outer approximation); the robust protocol step reduces to the nominal problem at the worst-case targeting probabilities.

Exact solve, times to proof and a duel with a heuristic, but no warm start and no stated time limit; the GREEDY opponent is built by the authors, and the predecessor's linearized heuristic and protocol (Becker et al. 2013) are compared only in words. The 98.9x headline uses time to the optimum (time to proof: about 32x, my arithmetic); nine parallel cut arms are not matched in compute.

An exact formulation described as intractable at 20 weapons x 20 threats is reopened by a device (lazy tangent cuts), with times measured up to 40 hard-kill weapons and 24 threats; no solver-speed figure and no concession step.
The message budget is offered to the decision maker as a knob for communication, but only a budget of 2 is run; no price curve.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: constraint generation as the scaling engine
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: LAZY drops the product constraints and adds closed-form tangent cuts (Lemma 1); nine cut variants race in parallel; time to the optimum 3.93 s against 389 s for the binary SOCP.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: report time to the hindsight-best solution separately from time to proof
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Tables 2-5 report first integer solution, optimal solution found and optimality proven separately; Table 4's 95% quantiles are read as a stop time with an optimality probability. Same device as S445 (card s2-10).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: communication as a budgeted decision variable
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Each ship's own MIO picks binary broadcast variables under a message budget; the untold part becomes box uncertainty in a robust re-solve; Proposition 1 shows no ship is worse off.

transferable: For a convex constraint gamma <= prod x_i (products of survival or leak probabilities), keep the MIP linear: drop the constraint and add the closed-form tangent cut sum x_i/yhat_i = n at a projected point; run several cut rules in parallel and stop at the first proof (pp. 9-10, 23, 41-42).

In a distributed protocol, let each agent's own optimization choose which facts to broadcast (binary message variables under a budget), then treat what was not said as box uncertainty whose robust counterpart is the nominal model at the upper bound (pp. 15-18).
Prove that a coordination round never hurts by showing that the first-round solution stays feasible in the second-round problem (p. 20; pp. 42-43).
Report 95% quantiles of time to the optimum and time to proof over many random instances, so that an operator can read off a stop time with an optimality probability (p. 24; Table 4, p. 37).
Bracket a decentralized method between the no-communication and the full-information centralized solutions on the same instances (Table 7, pp. 28-29, 40).
coauthors: Patrick Jaillet and Nikita Korolko (Operations Research Center, MIT; Korolko's listed e-mail is at Uber) (p. 1)

quotes.text: While this approach yields an optimal solution to the FDP that can serve as a benchmark, it cannot be used in real time.

If the survival threshold of ship s belongs, for instance, to the interval [0.9; 0.95] and the decision maker terminates the computation of the FDP after 0.6 s, then with 95 % probability the best integer solution found by this time is optimal.

title: Optimal Selection of Health Care Providers
contribution: A MILO that replays a self-insured employer's 2011-2015 claims in hindsight, reassigning patients to nearby lower-cost providers under capacity, travel and procedure-count limits; solved to optimality or within 0.23% on a region of more than 21,000 providers, it estimates about 10-11% lower procedure costs with half as many providers.
problem_entry: {IO DA AP} US health spending rises without better quality, driven in part by opaque, widely varying prices (pp. 1-3); a self-insured employer holds its claims and can identify low-cost providers near its patients (pp. 1, 4); the question is posed in hindsight: what would sending patients to nearby cheaper providers have saved, and which providers and procedures matter (pp. 7-9).
key_idea: One MILO (Formulation 1, p. 13) reassigns historical demand, procedure by procedure, to providers within distance delta, minimizing cost plus a penalty lambda per provider, with zip-to-zip flow variables, a budget phi on procedure types moved and capacities as multiples of observed volume (pp. 12-14); exact decomposition into connected components of the within-delta zip-code graph, with a counterexample against neighbourhood-by-neighbourhood solving (pp. 9-10).
assumptions: Claims paid 1 Jan 2011 - 1 Jul 2015 by a large self-insured southern US employer: 1.55 million claims, more than 14,000 patients, about 30,000 providers, 4,792 procedures, more than $151M (p. 5); cleaned with the CMS NPI file to about 520,000 rows and $82.5M (p. 8; pp. 30-31); procedures only (p. 9); largest region at delta = 50 km: about 77% of procedure costs, $63.6M over 3.5 years, more than 21,000 providers (p. 11). Perfect hindsight on demand and average prices (pp. 9, 12); prices floored at Medicare reference prices against data error; capacity = Dbar times historical volume for lack of capacity data (p. 12); quality treated as unchanged, argued from the many diagnostic procedures selected (p. 28).
proof_devices: exact decomposition into connected components of the within-delta zip-code graph (p. 9)
three-zip counterexample against neighbourhood-by-neighbourhood decomposition (p. 10)
aggregated zip-to-zip flow variables, with constraints only for (procedure, zip) pairs present in the data: about 177,000 constraints and 184,000 variables (pp. 13-14)
data-derived big-M values M1 = D(Dbar - 1), M2 = D for the procedure-budget constraints (p. 13)
per-provider penalty lambda as an implicit cardinality knob; lambda = 0 gives the cheapest provider per procedure (pp. 14-15)
Medicare price floor and capacity multiple as conservative input guards (p. 12)
experiments: Julia/JuMP, Gurobi 6.5.0, quad-core i7-3770 with 32 GB (pp. 14-15); 360 settings of (lambda, phi, Dbar, delta) at 600 s each: 240 proved optimal, the rest within 0.23% (all with lambda >= 2000), gaps under 1% within two minutes (p. 15). Baseline: the $63.6M actually paid in the region; no competing method (pp. 16-17). Headline: $56.8M (about 11% less) with half as many providers at delta = 40 km, Dbar = 2.5, phi = 100, lambda = 1000 (p. 21). One-at-a-time sensitivity in delta, phi, lambda and Dbar (pp. 17-22); colonoscopy/biopsy drill-down: average $1,279 to $825 for 284 patients, 141 stay in their zip code, the others travel 13 km median and 18.1 km mean, 10 of 149 providers at full assumed capacity (pp. 22-26). No hold-out evaluation, no field test.
positioning: Positioned in health policy rather than OR: the ten references are health-economics, policy and news sources plus Julia/JuMP (p. 31); the model is called related to minimum vertex cover without citation (p. 11); no facility-location or network-design work and none of his own claims-data papers (e.g. DOI 10.1287/opre.1080.0619) are cited (p. 31).
writing: MSOM structured abstract (Problem definition, Academic/Practical Relevance, Methodology, Results, Managerial implications) (p. 1); 'conservative' attached to the 10% throughout (pp. 1, 19, 21, 28); a policy section turning the optimum into actions (pp. 27-28); internal inconsistencies on the horizon, the time limit and a provider count (pp. 15, 16-17, 25, 27).
limits_future: Admitted: no capacity data (p. 12); about 10% of cost discarded in cleaning (p. 30); travel not penalized in the objective (p. 24); results 'just the first step' (p. 27). My reading: in-sample perfect-hindsight replay (p. 9); quality only argued (p. 28); the abstract's 18 km (40 km) travel figures are the colonoscopy movers' mean and the 40 km cap, and its 10% refers to procedure costs in the largest region (pp. 1, 9, 11, 24, 28); slips on the horizon (4 vs 3.5 years, pp. 16-17), the time limit (600 vs 500 s, p. 15) and providers above 5 extra procedures (7 vs 4, pp. 25, 27). Future: a per-km travel penalty (p. 24), negotiation and minimum-volume contracts with the selected providers (pp. 8, 28), side constraints (p. 29).

method_links.note: Owner (self-insured employer), its own claims, baseline = what it actually paid; the decision is scored in dollars beside patient travel and provider load, and the paper closes with implementable policies (provider lists, copay incentives, service contracts). No field test; the replay is in-sample.
Provider selection written as one MILO kept tractable by an exact component decomposition and a sparse zip-to-zip flow form, with solve times measured on the real instance.
Solver, version, machine, 600 s limit, certificates for 240 of 360 settings and the worst gap (0.23%) are reported; no warm start and no duel with another method, only with history.

The convenience-cost trade-off is priced by knobs (lambda per provider, delta for travel, phi for procedure types), with knees read off the curves (phi about 200; lambda = 1000); no bound, and the sensitivity varies one knob at a time.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: counterfactual replay against the historical decision-maker
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Patients' historical procedures are reassigned in perfect hindsight and the cost is compared with the $63.6M actually paid in the region; prices and volumes come from the same claims, so the replay is in-sample.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact decomposition by connected components, with a counterexample to local decomposition
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Regions are connected components of the within-delta zip-code graph and are solved separately without loss; a three-zip example shows that a price change two hops away moves the optimum, so neighbourhood-by-neighbourhood solving is not exact.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: conservative input guards so the headline saving is understated
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Average prices are floored at the Medicare reference price against data error, capacity is a small multiple of observed volume, and the 10% is called conservative, with up to 15% if parameters are relaxed.

transferable: Split a reassignment problem into the connected components of its eligibility graph, which loses nothing, and show with a two-hop counterexample why solving each neighbourhood alone is not exact (pp. 9-10).
When capacity data are missing, set capacity to a multiple of observed volume, sweep the multiple, and explain the jumps that integrality produces (pp. 12, 21-22, 25).
Guard against data errors in the direction that shrinks the claimed saving: floor estimated unit prices at a public reference price (p. 12).
Report the solve protocol over the whole parameter grid: the time limit, how many settings were proved optimal, the worst remaining gap and which parameter drives the hardness (p. 15).
Show the owner the users' burden beside the saving, for a representative procedure: price histograms, travel histograms and each provider's added load (pp. 22-27).

quotes.text: For our analysis, we formulate a model whose solution represents perfect hindsight; that is, given the historical claims data that we have collected so far, we consider the optimal re-assignment of patients to nearby low-cost providers.
In 240 of the parameter settings, provable optimality was achieved within the time limit.
